concept.title: What Is Phishing?
concept.shortdesc: Phishing is a social engineering attack in which criminals impersonate trusted people or organizations to steal credentials, financial data, or university information.

conbody.p: According to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), phishing uses deceptive emails, text messages, phone calls, or shared documents to trick recipients into clicking malicious links, opening infected attachments, or revealing sensitive information such as Unity passwords and Duo two-factor authentication (2FA) codes.

ul.li: Bulk Phishing: Broad, untargeted emails sent to thousands of recipients pretending to be a bank, shipping carrier, or university IT service.

Spear Phishing: Targeted messages customized for a specific individual, department, or role—such as fake student job offers, fraudulent payroll or pension updates, or messages impersonating NC State faculty and leadership.
Smishing (SMS Phishing): Fraudulent text messages sent to mobile phones containing malicious links or urgent requests for personal details.
Vishing (Voice Phishing): Phone calls or voicemails in which scammers pose as technical support, financial institutions, or government agencies.

section.title: Warning Signs of a Phishing Scam

ul.li: Urgent or Threatening Language: Claims that your NC State Unity account will be suspended or locked unless you act immediately.
Mismatched Sender Addresses: Display names that look familiar, paired with an external or misspelled email domain.
Suspicious Login URLs: Links leading to look-alike login pages. Authentic NC State single sign-on pages always start with shib.ncsu.edu or login.microsoftonline.com.
Requests for Credentials or Bypass Codes: Unexpected prompts asking for your Unity password, Duo 2FA approval, or financial information.
Offers That Seem Too Good to Be True: Unsolicited part-time job offers, grant awards, or gift card requests.

section.note: NC State Office of Information Technology (OIT) personnel will never ask for your Unity password or Duo 2FA bypass codes via email, text message, or phone.
